Cover the background on PINNs and PINOs, why coordinate derivatives matter, what has been overlooked, our contribution, and the paper's structure.

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
- Physics-informed ML, PINNs, PINOs
  - framework for emulation and inversion of PDEs; extends to stochastic, integro-differential, fractional differential equations
  - originated from PINNs: learn map x\mapsto u (x = coordinates of collocation points from domain, u = solution field)
  - PINN limitation: no generalisability over variation of physical parameters (material properties, external sources, initial and boundary conditions)
  - motivates PINOs: DeepONets, physics-informed FNOs; learn p(x)\mapsto u(x), p(x) = physical parameter of interest
  - PINN: map between two vector spaces; PINO: map between two function spaces; PINO degenerates to PINN for invariant p(x)
- "Physics-informed" and derivatives
  - meaning: embed target PDE + initial/boundary conditions into loss function
  - helps network understand physics, not just fit data -> lower generalisation error with less training data
  - PDE loss and non-Dirichlet boundary conditions need high-order derivatives of output w.r.t. coordinates
  - e.g. bending of elastic plate, stream function for incompressible 2-D fluids: fourth-order PDE
  - gradient of PDE itself as stronger regularisation -> even higher orders
  - automatic differentiation (AD): pivotal for deep learning; major facilitator of physics-informed ML
- Prior advances and the gap
  - since modern PINNs: multi-scale / multi-frequency models, domain decomposition, adaptive activation functions, data sampling, physics as hard constraints
  - less attention to AD; coordinate derivatives differ from backpropagation (gradient of loss w.r.t. network weights) in many ways
  - full survey in next section
- ZCS
  - reshapes AD for operator learning; reduces GPU memory and training wall time by an order of magnitude
  - one scalar-valued leaf variable per dimension: "many-roots-many-leaves" -> "one-root-many-leaves"; exploit reverse-mode AD
  - lower level than network, agnostic to forward pass; no restrictions on data, point sampling, architecture
  - simple implementation: extends DeepXDE with a few overridden methods
- Organization
  - Section 2: related work review; Section 3: theory and implementation
  - Section 4: experiments (benchmark scaling, PDE operators learned without data)
  - Section 5: limitations; Section 6: conclusions

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Physics-informed machine learning is a versatile framework for emulating and inverting partial differential equations (PDEs) in physics, and it can be extended to other kinds of differential equations like stochastic differential equations, integro-differential equations, and fractional differential equations. This deep learning-based paradigm came from the physics-informed neural networks (PINNs), which are targeted at learning a map x\mapsto u, where x is the coordinates of the collocation points sampled from the domain and u is the solution field. A built-in limitation of PINNs is that they do not generalise over variation of physical parameters, such as material properties, external sources, and initial and boundary conditions. This limitation motivated the physics-informed neural operators (PINOs), for example the deep operator networks (DeepONets) and the physics-informed Fourier neural operators (FNOs), which learn a map p(x)\mapsto u(x), where p(x) is any physical parameter of interest. So basically PINNs learn a map between two vector spaces and PINOs learn a map between two function spaces, and in many contexts a PINO becomes a PINN if p(x) is invariant.

The term "physics-informed" in PINNs and PINOs has a specific meaning, which is embedding the target PDE and its initial and boundary conditions into the loss function. This embedded information is supposed to help a neural network understand the underlying physics (and not just fit data) so it can get a lower generalisation error with less training data. To compute the loss functions for a PDE and for any of its non-Dirichlet boundary conditions, you need the high-order derivatives of the network output w.r.t. the coordinates. For example, bending of an elastic plate and the stream function for incompressible 2-D fluids both involve a fourth-order PDE. Also, the gradient of the PDE itself can be used as an even stronger regularisation, which makes the required orders of derivatives even higher. Automatic differentiation (AD) is a powerful tool for computing derivatives, and it is a pivotal technique behind deep learning today and one of the major things that made physics-informed machine learning possible.

- Prior advances and the gap
  - since modern PINNs: multi-scale / multi-frequency models, domain decomposition, adaptive activation functions, data sampling, physics as hard constraints
  - less attention to AD; coordinate derivatives differ from backpropagation (gradient of loss w.r.t. network weights)
  - full survey in next section
- ZCS
  - reshapes AD for operator learning; GPU memory and training wall time reduced by an order of magnitude
  - one scalar-valued leaf variable per dimension: "many-roots-many-leaves" -> "one-root-many-leaves"; reverse-mode AD
  - agnostic to forward pass; no restrictions on data, point sampling, architecture
  - implemented by extending DeepXDE with a few overridden methods
- Organization
  - Section 2 related work; Section 3 theory and implementation; Section 4 experiments (scaling benchmark, operators learned without data); Section 5 limitations; Section 6 conclusions

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Physics-informed machine learning is a versatile framework for emulating and inverting partial differential equations (PDEs) in physics, and it can be extended to other kinds of differential equations like stochastic differential equations, integro-differential equations, and fractional differential equations. This deep learning-based paradigm came from the physics-informed neural networks (PINNs), which are targeted at learning a map x\mapsto u, where x is the coordinates of the collocation points sampled from the domain and u is the solution field. A built-in limitation of PINNs is that they do not generalise over variation of physical parameters, such as material properties, external sources, and initial and boundary conditions. This limitation motivated the physics-informed neural operators (PINOs), for example the deep operator networks (DeepONets) and the physics-informed Fourier neural operators (FNOs), which learn a map p(x)\mapsto u(x), where p(x) is any physical parameter of interest. So basically PINNs learn a map between two vector spaces and PINOs learn a map between two function spaces, and in many contexts a PINO becomes a PINN if p(x) is invariant.

The term "physics-informed" in PINNs and PINOs has a specific meaning, which is embedding the target PDE and its initial and boundary conditions into the loss function. This embedded information is supposed to help a neural network understand the underlying physics (and not just fit data) so it can get a lower generalisation error with less training data. To compute the loss functions for a PDE and for any of its non-Dirichlet boundary conditions, you need the high-order derivatives of the network output w.r.t. the coordinates. For example, bending of an elastic plate and the stream function for incompressible 2-D fluids both involve a fourth-order PDE. Also, the gradient of the PDE itself can be used as an even stronger regularisation, which makes the required orders of derivatives even higher. Automatic differentiation (AD) is a powerful tool for computing derivatives, and it is a pivotal technique behind deep learning today and one of the major things that made physics-informed machine learning possible.

There have been many technical advancements since modern PINNs were established, for example multi-scale and multi-frequency models, domain decomposition techniques, adaptive activation functions and data sampling, and embedding physics as hard constraints. Even with all these efforts, we think less attention has been paid to AD, especially since the coordinate derivatives in physics-informed machine learning are different in many ways from the well-known backpropagation (computing the gradient of the loss function w.r.t. network weights). We will give a comprehensive survey of related work in the next section.

In this paper we present a new algorithm that reshapes AD for operator learning, and it can reduce both GPU memory consumption and wall time for training by an order of magnitude. We call our algorithm Zero Coordinate Shift (ZCS). It introduces one scalar-valued leaf variable for each dimension, which simplifies the coordinate derivatives we want from "many-roots-many-leaves" to "one-root-many-leaves", so that reverse-mode AD, the most powerful mode, can be exploited as much as possible. The algorithm is at a lower level than the neural network (it is agnostic to the forward pass), so it puts no restrictions on data, point sampling or network architecture. Also, ZCS is straightforward to implement; we implemented it by extending the DeepXDE package with only a few overridden methods.

The rest of the paper is organised as follows. Section 2 gives a more detailed review of related work to further justify our motivation. Section 3 describes the theory and implementation of ZCS. Section 4 reports our experiments, including a benchmark analysis showing the scaling behaviours of ZCS and a few PDE operators learned without data. Section 5 describes the limitations we identified, and Section 6 concludes the paper.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
Physics-informed machine learning offers a versatile framework for the emulation and inversion of partial differential equations (PDEs) in physics [1,2], and it is extensible to other types of differential equations such as stochastic differential equations [3], integro-differential equations [4], and fractional differential equations [5]. This deep learning-based paradigm originated from the physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) [6,7,8,9], which target learning a map x\mapsto u, with x being the coordinates of the collocation points sampled from the domain and u the solution field. An innate limitation of PINNs is that they cannot generalise over the variation of physical parameters, such as material properties, external sources, and initial and boundary conditions. This limitation has motivated the physics-informed neural operators (PINOs), such as the deep operator networks (DeepONets) [10] and the physics-informed Fourier neural operators (FNOs) [11], which learn a map p(x)\mapsto u(x), with p(x) being any physical parameter of interest. In short, PINNs learn a map between two vector spaces and PINOs a map between two function spaces; in many contexts, a PINO degenerates to a PINN given an invariant p(x).

The term "physics-informed" in PINNs and PINOs has a specific meaning: embedding the target PDE and its initial and boundary conditions into the loss function. This embedded information is supposed to help a neural network understand the underlying physics (rather than just fit data) and thereby achieve a lower generalisation error with less training data. To compute the loss functions associated with a PDE and any of its non-Dirichlet boundary conditions, one needs the high-order derivatives of the network output w.r.t. the coordinates. For example, bending of an elastic plate and the stream function for incompressible 2-D fluids both involve a fourth-order PDE. Moreover, the gradient of the PDE itself may serve as an even stronger regularisation [12], which further increases the required orders of derivatives. A powerful tool for computing derivatives is automatic differentiation (AD), a pivotal technique behind today's deep learning [13,14,15,16] and one of the major facilitators of physics-informed machine learning [1,2,9].

Technical advancements have flourished since the establishment of modern PINNs [8,9], e.g., multi-scale and multi-frequency models [17,18], domain decomposition techniques [19,20], adaptive activation functions [21] and data sampling [22,23], and embedding physics as hard constraints [24,25,26]. Despite these continuing efforts, we feel that less attention has been paid to AD, especially given that the coordinate derivatives in physics-informed machine learning differ in many ways from the well-known backpropagation (i.e., calculating the gradient of the loss function w.r.t. network weights). A comprehensive survey of related work is provided in the next section.

In this paper, we present a novel algorithm that reshapes AD for operator learning, reducing both GPU memory consumption and wall time for training by an order of magnitude. Our algorithm, which we call Zero Coordinate Shift (ZCS), introduces one scalar-valued leaf variable for each dimension, simplifying the wanted coordinate derivatives from "many-roots-many-leaves" to "one-root-many-leaves" so that the most powerful reverse-mode AD can be exploited to the maximum. Our algorithm lies at a lower level than the neural network (i.e., it is agnostic to the forward pass) and imposes no restrictions on data, point sampling or network architecture. Furthermore, ZCS is straightforward to implement; our own implementation extends the DeepXDE package [27] with only a few overridden methods.

The remainder of this paper is organised as follows. In Section 2, we provide a more detailed review of the related work to further justify our motivation. In Section 3, we describe the theory and implementation of ZCS. We report our experiments in Section 4, including a benchmark analysis exhibiting the scaling behaviours of ZCS and a few PDE operators learned without data. Identified limitations are described in Section 5, and the paper is concluded in Section 6.
